tname: Introduction to limits and the derivative as gradient / rate of change
text:
Let $f(x)=x^2-3x$. The points $P(2,\,-2)$ and $Q\big(2+h,\ f(2+h)\big)$, where $h\neq 0$, lie on the graph of $f$.

(a) Show that the gradient of the chord $PQ$ is $1+h$. [3]

(b) By considering the limit as $h\to 0$, write down the gradient of the tangent to the graph of $f$ at $P$. [1]
ms:
**(a)** $f(2+h)=(2+h)^2-3(2+h)$ **(M1)**

$=4+4h+h^2-6-3h=h^2+h-2$ **A1**

gradient of $PQ=\dfrac{(h^2+h-2)-(-2)}{(2+h)-2}=\dfrac{h^2+h}{h}=\dfrac{h(h+1)}{h}$ **M1**

$=1+h$ **AG**

Note: award **M1** for a correct substitution into $\dfrac{y_2-y_1}{x_2-x_1}$ with their $f(2+h)$.

**(b)** as $h\to 0$, $1+h\to 1$, so the gradient of the tangent at $P$ is $1$ **A1**

[Total 4 marks]

tname: Introduction to limits and the derivative as gradient / rate of change
text:
Water is pumped into a tank. The volume of water in the tank, $V$ litres, $t$ minutes after pumping starts is given by
$$V(t)=200+30t-t^2,\quad 0\le t\le 20.$$

(a) Find the average rate of change of $V$ between $t=2$ and $t=6$. [2]

(b) Find $V'(t)$. [1]

(c) Find the rate at which the volume is changing when $t=6$. [1]

(d) Find the value of $t$ at which the instantaneous rate of change of $V$ is equal to the average rate of change of $V$ over the interval $0\le t\le 20$. [3]
ms:
**(a)** $V(2)=256,\ V(6)=344$ **(A1)**

average rate $=\dfrac{344-256}{6-2}=22\ \text{L min}^{-1}$ **A1**

**(b)** $V'(t)=30-2t$ **A1**

**(c)** $V'(6)=30-12=18\ \text{L min}^{-1}$ **A1**

Note: units not required.

**(d)** average rate over $0\le t\le 20$: $\dfrac{V(20)-V(0)}{20}=\dfrac{400-200}{20}=10$ **(M1)(A1)**

$30-2t=10\Rightarrow t=10$ (minutes) **A1**

Note: **FT** from their average rate and their $V'(t)$.

[Total 7 marks]

tname: Introduction to limits and the derivative as gradient / rate of change
text:
The following diagram shows part of the graph of $y=f(x)$. The points $A$, $B$, $C$ and $P(4,\,3)$ lie on the graph. The line $L$ is the tangent to the graph at $P$, and $L$ passes through the point $(2,\,-1)$.

![graph of y = f(x) with points A, B, C, P and tangent L at P through (2, -1)](qbank/img/gen_math_SL5.1_3.svg)

(a) Find the gradient of $L$. [2]

(b) Hence write down the value of $\displaystyle\lim_{h\to 0}\frac{f(4+h)-f(4)}{h}$. [1]

(c) State, with a reason, whether $f'(x)$ is positive or negative at $B$. [2]
ms:
**(a)** gradient $=\dfrac{3-(-1)}{4-2}$ **(M1)**

$=2$ **A1**

**(b)** the limit is $f'(4)$, the gradient of the tangent at $P$: $2$ **A1**

Note: **FT** their answer to (a).

**(c)** negative **A1**

the graph of $f$ is decreasing at $B$ (the tangent at $B$ slopes downwards) **R1**

Note: do not award **A1R0**.

[Total 5 marks]

tname: Increasing and decreasing functions, graphical interpretation of f'(x)
text:
Let $f(x)=x^3-3x^2-2x+1$.

(a) Find $f'(x)$. [1]

(b) Find the set of values of $x$ for which $f$ is decreasing. [4]
ms:
**(a)** $f'(x)=3x^2-6x-2$ **A1**

**(b)** recognizing $f$ decreasing when $f'(x)<0$ **(M1)**

solving $3x^2-6x-2=0$: $x=-0.291,\ x=2.29$ **(A1)(A1)**

(exact values $x=1\pm\dfrac{\sqrt{15}}{3}$)

$-0.291<x<2.29$ **A1**

Note: accept $-0.291\le x\le 2.29$. **FT** from their $f'(x)$.

[Total 5 marks]

tname: Increasing and decreasing functions, graphical interpretation of f'(x)
text:
The function $f$ is defined for $-3\le x\le 4$. The following diagram shows the graph of $y=f'(x)$, the **derivative** of $f$. The graph of $f'$ crosses the $x$-axis at $x=-2$, $x=1$ and $x=3$.

![graph of y = f'(x) crossing the x-axis at -2, 1 and 3](qbank/img/gen_math_SL5.2_2.svg)

(a) Write down the intervals for which $f$ is decreasing. [2]

(b) Find the $x$-coordinate of the local maximum point on the graph of $f$. Justify your answer. [2]

(c) Explain why $f(3)<f(1)$. [2]
ms:
**(a)** $-3\le x<-2$ **A1**

$1<x<3$ **A1**

Note: accept $-3<x<-2$ and inequalities including endpoints.

**(b)** $x=1$ **A1**

$f'(x)$ changes from positive to negative at $x=1$ **R1**

Note: do not award **A1R0**. Do not accept $x=-2$ or $x=3$ (these are local minima, where $f'$ changes from negative to positive).

**(c)** $f'(x)<0$ for $1<x<3$ **R1**

so $f$ is decreasing on this interval, hence $f(3)<f(1)$ **R1**

[Total 6 marks]

tname: Increasing and decreasing functions, graphical interpretation of f'(x)
text:
Let $f(x)=\ln(x^2+1)-\dfrac{x}{2}$, for $x\in\mathbb{R}$.

(a) Find $f'(x)$. [2]

(b) Find the interval in which $f$ is increasing. [3]
ms:
**(a)** $f'(x)=\dfrac{2x}{x^2+1}-\dfrac12$ **A1A1**

Note: award **A1** for $\dfrac{2x}{x^2+1}$ (chain rule) and **A1** for $-\dfrac12$.

**(b)** $f'(x)>0$ **(M1)**

$f'(x)=0$ at $x=0.268$ and $x=3.73$ (exact $2\pm\sqrt3$) **(A1)**

$0.268<x<3.73$ **A1**

Note: accept $\le$. **FT** from their $f'(x)$ provided it is not a constant.

[Total 5 marks]

tname: Increasing and decreasing functions, graphical interpretation of f'(x)
text:
Let $f(x)=x^3+kx^2+3x-2$, where $k\in\mathbb{R}$.

Given that $f$ is an increasing function for all $x\in\mathbb{R}$, find the set of possible values of $k$. [6]
ms:
$f'(x)=3x^2+2kx+3$ **A1**

$f$ increasing for all $x\Rightarrow f'(x)\ge 0$ for all $x$ **R1**

the quadratic $f'(x)$ has at most one (repeated) root, so discriminant $\le 0$ **(M1)**

$(2k)^2-4(3)(3)\le 0$ **A1**

$4k^2\le 36\Rightarrow k^2\le 9$ **(A1)**

$-3\le k\le 3$ **A1**

Note: accept $-3<k<3$ (when $k=\pm3$, $f'(x)=3(x\pm1)^2\ge0$, which is zero at only one point, so $f$ is still increasing). Award **A0** for $k\le 3$ only or $k=\pm3$.

[Total 6 marks]

tname: Derivative of ax^n; derivative of polynomials
text:
Let $f(x)=2x^4-3x^2+\dfrac{6}{x}$, $x\neq 0$.

(a) Find $f'(x)$. [3]

(b) Find the gradient of the graph of $f$ at the point where $x=-1$. [2]

tname: Derivative of ax^n; derivative of polynomials
text:
Let $f(x)=0.4x^3-2.5x^2+3x+1$.

(a) Find $f'(x)$. [2]

(b) Find the values of $x$ for which the gradient of the graph of $f$ is equal to $1$. [3]

tname: Derivative of ax^n; derivative of polynomials
text:
Let $f(x)=ax^2+\dfrac{b}{x}$, $x\neq0$, where $a,\,b\in\mathbb{R}$. The graph of $f$ passes through the point $(1,\,17)$, and the gradient of the graph at this point is $-14$.

(a) Show that $a+b=17$. [1]

(b) Find $f'(x)$ in terms of $a$ and $b$. [2]

(c) Find the value of $a$ and the value of $b$. [3]

(d) Find the coordinates of the point on the graph of $f$ at which the tangent is horizontal. [3]
ms:
**(a)** $f(1)=a(1)^2+\dfrac{b}{1}=17\Rightarrow a+b=17$ **A1AG**

**(b)** $f(x)=ax^2+bx^{-1}$

$f'(x)=2ax-bx^{-2}\ \left(=2ax-\dfrac{b}{x^2}\right)$ **A1A1**

**(c)** $f'(1)=-14\Rightarrow 2a-b=-14$ **(M1)**

solving simultaneously with $a+b=17$: $3a=3$ **(M1)**

$a=1,\ b=16$ **A1**

**(d)** $f'(x)=2x-\dfrac{16}{x^2}=0$ **(M1)**

$x^3=8\Rightarrow x=2$ **A1**

$f(2)=4+8=12$, point $(2,\,12)$ **A1**

Note: **FT** from their values of $a$ and $b$.

[Total 9 marks]

tname: Tangents and normals
text:
Let $f(x)=x^3-2x+1$.

(a) Find $f'(x)$. [1]

(b) Find the equation of the tangent to the graph of $f$ at the point where $x=2$. [3]

(c) The tangent meets the graph of $f$ again at the point $Q$. Find the $x$-coordinate of $Q$. [2]
ms:
**(a)** $f'(x)=3x^2-2$ **A1**

**(b)** $f(2)=5$ **(A1)**

$f'(2)=10$ **(A1)**

$y-5=10(x-2)$ or $y=10x-15$ **A1**

**(c)** $x^3-2x+1=10x-15$ (or using GDC to find intersection) **(M1)**

$x=-4$ **A1**

Note: $x^3-12x+16=(x-2)^2(x+4)=0$. **FT** from their tangent if the resulting equation has a second root.

[Total 6 marks]

tname: Tangents and normals
text:
The following diagram shows part of the graph of $y=x^2-4x+5$. The point $A(3,\,2)$ lies on the graph. The normal to the graph at $A$ meets the graph again at $B$.

![parabola y = x^2 - 4x + 5 with the normal at A(3, 2) meeting the curve again at B](qbank/img/gen_math_SL5.4_2.svg)

(a) Show that the equation of the normal at $A$ is $x+2y=7$. [4]

(b) Find the coordinates of $B$. [3]
ms:
**(a)** $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=2x-4$ **A1**

at $x=3$, gradient of tangent $=2$ **A1**

gradient of normal $=-\dfrac12$ **(M1)**

$y-2=-\dfrac12(x-3)\Rightarrow 2y-4=-x+3$ **A1**

$x+2y=7$ **AG**

**(b)** $x^2-4x+5=\dfrac{7-x}{2}$ **M1**

$2x^2-7x+3=0\Rightarrow(2x-1)(x-3)=0$ **(A1)**

$x=\dfrac12$, so $B\left(\dfrac12,\ \dfrac{13}{4}\right)$ **A1**

[Total 7 marks]

tname: Tangents and normals
text:
Let $f(x)=\ln(2x+1)+x$, for $x>-\dfrac12$.

(a) Find $f'(x)$. [2]

(b) Find the equation of the tangent to the graph of $f$ at the point where $x=2$. Give your answer in the form $y=mx+c$. [2]

(c) The tangent meets the $x$-axis at $A$ and the $y$-axis at $B$. Find the area of triangle $OAB$, where $O$ is the origin. [2]

tname: Tangents and normals
text:
The line $y=mx$ is a tangent to the curve $y=x^2-2x+9$.

(a) Find the two possible values of $m$. [5]

(b) For the positive value of $m$, find the coordinates of the point where the line touches the curve. [2]
ms:
**METHOD 1**

**(a)** $x^2-2x+9=mx\Rightarrow x^2-(2+m)x+9=0$ **M1**

tangent so exactly one solution: discriminant $=0$ **(R1)**

$(2+m)^2-36=0$ **A1**

$2+m=\pm6$ **(A1)**

$m=4$ or $m=-8$ **A1**

**METHOD 2**

point of contact $(a,\ a^2-2a+9)$, gradient $2a-2$ **(M1)**

line through origin: $a^2-2a+9=a(2a-2)$ **(R1)A1**

$a^2=9\Rightarrow a=\pm3$ **(A1)**

$m=2(3)-2=4$ or $m=2(-3)-2=-8$ **A1**

**(b)** $x^2-6x+9=0\Rightarrow x=3$ **(A1)**

$(3,\,12)$ **A1**

[Total 7 marks]

tname: Tangents and normals
text:
Let $f(x)=2\mathrm{e}^{0.5x}$. The point $P$ on the graph of $f$ has $x$-coordinate $1$.

(a) Find the gradient of the normal to the graph of $f$ at $P$. [2]

(b) Find the equation of the normal at $P$. [2]

(c) The normal meets the $x$-axis at $Q$. Find the $x$-coordinate of $Q$. [2]

tname: Introduction to integration, anti-differentiation, area between curve and x-axis
text:
(a) Find $\displaystyle\int\left(6x^2-4x+3\right)\,\mathrm{d}x$. [3]

(b) Given that $f'(x)=6x^2-4x+3$ and $f(1)=5$, find $f(x)$. [2]
ms:
**(a)** $2x^3-2x^2+3x+C$ **A1A1A1**

Note: award **A1** for each correct term; condone absence of $+C$ here.

**(b)** $2(1)^3-2(1)^2+3(1)+C=5$ **(M1)**

$C=2$, so $f(x)=2x^3-2x^2+3x+2$ **A1**

[Total 5 marks]

tname: Introduction to integration, anti-differentiation, area between curve and x-axis
text:
The following diagram shows part of the graph of $y=4x-x^2$. The shaded region is enclosed by the graph and the $x$-axis.

![graph of y = 4x - x^2 with the region between the curve and the x-axis shaded](qbank/img/gen_math_SL5.5_2.svg)

(a) Find the $x$-intercepts of the graph. [2]

(b) Find the area of the shaded region. [4]
ms:
**(a)** $x(4-x)=0$ **(M1)**

$x=0,\ x=4$ **A1**

**(b)** area $=\displaystyle\int_0^4\left(4x-x^2\right)\mathrm{d}x$ **(M1)**

$=\left[2x^2-\dfrac{x^3}{3}\right]_0^4$ **A1A1**

$=32-\dfrac{64}{3}=\dfrac{32}{3}$ **A1**

[Total 6 marks]

tname: Introduction to integration, anti-differentiation, area between curve and x-axis
text:
Let $f(x)=-0.2x^3+x^2+1$. The following diagram shows part of the graph of $f$, which crosses the positive $x$-axis at $A$. The shaded region $R$ is enclosed by the graph of $f$, the $x$-axis and the $y$-axis.

![cubic graph crossing the positive x-axis at A, region R under the curve shaded](qbank/img/gen_math_SL5.5_3.svg)

(a) Find the $x$-coordinate of $A$. [2]

(b) (i) Write down an integral which represents the area of $R$.

(ii) Find the area of $R$. [3]
ms:
**(a)** $-0.2x^3+x^2+1=0$ (using GDC) **(M1)**

$x=5.19$ **A1**

**(b)(i)** $\displaystyle\int_0^{5.19}\left(-0.2x^3+x^2+1\right)\mathrm{d}x$ **A1A1**

Note: award **A1** for correct limits and **A1** for correct integrand. Condone absence of $\mathrm{d}x$.

**(ii)** $15.5$ **A1**

Note: **FT** from their (i). Answer from using $5.19$ instead of $5.1859\ldots$ is $15.5$.

[Total 5 marks]

tname: Introduction to integration, anti-differentiation, area between curve and x-axis
text:
Let $f(x)=x^2-3x$. The following diagram shows part of the graph of $f$. The shaded regions $A$ and $B$ are enclosed by the graph of $f$, the $x$-axis and the line $x=4$.

![graph of y = x^2 - 3x; region A below the x-axis between 0 and 3, region B above between 3 and 4](qbank/img/gen_math_SL5.5_4.svg)

(a) Find $\displaystyle\int_0^4 f(x)\,\mathrm{d}x$. [3]

(b) Explain why your answer to part (a) is not the total area of the shaded regions. [1]

(c) Find the total area of the shaded regions. [3]
ms:
**(a)** $\left[\dfrac{x^3}{3}-\dfrac{3x^2}{2}\right]_0^4$ **A1**

$=\dfrac{64}{3}-24$ **(A1)**

$=-\dfrac83$ **A1**

**(b)** region $A$ is below the $x$-axis, so its integral is negative and partly cancels the (positive) integral for $B$ **R1**

**(c)** $\displaystyle\int_0^3 f(x)\,\mathrm{d}x=9-\dfrac{27}{2}=-\dfrac92$, so area of $A=\dfrac92$ **(M1)(A1)**

area of $B=-\dfrac83-\left(-\dfrac92\right)=\dfrac{11}{6}$

total area $=\dfrac92+\dfrac{11}{6}=\dfrac{19}{3}$ **A1**

[Total 7 marks]

tname: Derivatives of x^n, sin, cos, e^x, ln x; chain, product and quotient rules
text:
Find the derivative of each of the following.

(a) $f(x)=4\ln x-3\cos x$, $x>0$ [2]

(b) $g(x)=\mathrm{e}^{2x+1}$ [2]
ms:
**(a)** $f'(x)=\dfrac4x+3\sin x$ **A1A1**

**(b)** $g'(x)=2\mathrm{e}^{2x+1}$ **A2**

Note: award **A1** for $\mathrm{e}^{2x+1}$ with an incorrect or missing factor.

[Total 4 marks]

tname: Derivatives of x^n, sin, cos, e^x, ln x; chain, product and quotient rules
text:
Let $f(x)=x^2\mathrm{e}^{-x}$.

(a) Find $f'(x)$. [2]

(b) Find the gradient of the graph of $f$ at the point where $x=0.5$. [1]

(c) Find the values of $x$ for which the gradient of the graph of $f$ is $0.2$. [3]
ms:
**(a)** product rule: $f'(x)=2x\mathrm{e}^{-x}-x^2\mathrm{e}^{-x}$ **A1A1**

Note: award **A1** for $2x\mathrm{e}^{-x}$ and **A1** for $-x^2\mathrm{e}^{-x}$.

**(b)** $0.455$ **A1**

**(c)** $2x\mathrm{e}^{-x}-x^2\mathrm{e}^{-x}=0.2$ **(M1)**

$x=0.120,\ x=1.42$ **A1A1**

Note: **FT** from their (a).

[Total 6 marks]

tname: Derivatives of x^n, sin, cos, e^x, ln x; chain, product and quotient rules
text:
Let $f(x)=\dfrac{\ln x}{x}$, $x>0$.

(a) Show that $f'(x)=\dfrac{1-\ln x}{x^2}$. [3]

(b) Find the exact value of $x$ for which $f'(x)=0$. [2]
ms:
**(a)** attempt to use the quotient rule **M1**

$f'(x)=\dfrac{x\cdot\frac1x-\ln x\cdot1}{x^2}$ **A1A1**

$=\dfrac{1-\ln x}{x^2}$ **AG**

Note: award **A1** for each correct term in the numerator. Accept product rule on $x^{-1}\ln x$.

**(b)** $1-\ln x=0$ **(M1)**

$x=\mathrm{e}$ **A1**

[Total 5 marks]

tname: Derivatives of x^n, sin, cos, e^x, ln x; chain, product and quotient rules
text:
Find the derivative of each of the following.

(a) $f(x)=(2x-1)^5$ [2]

(b) $g(x)=\sin\left(x^2\right)$ [2]

(c) Let $h(x)=\ln(\cos x)$, for $-\dfrac{\pi}{2}<x<\dfrac{\pi}{2}$. Show that $h'(x)=-\tan x$. [2]
ms:
**(a)** $f'(x)=5(2x-1)^4\times2=10(2x-1)^4$ **A1A1**

**(b)** $g'(x)=2x\cos\left(x^2\right)$ **A1A1**

Note: award **A1** for $\cos\left(x^2\right)$ and **A1** for the factor $2x$.

**(c)** $h'(x)=\dfrac{1}{\cos x}\times(-\sin x)$ **M1A1**

$=-\dfrac{\sin x}{\cos x}=-\tan x$ **AG**

[Total 6 marks]

tname: Derivatives of x^n, sin, cos, e^x, ln x; chain, product and quotient rules
text:
The functions $f$ and $g$ are differentiable. The following table gives some values of $f$, $g$ and their derivatives.

| $x$ | $f(x)$ | $f'(x)$ | $g(x)$ | $g'(x)$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| $1$ | $3$ | $-2$ | $2$ | $4$ |
| $2$ | $5$ | $1$ | $1$ | $-3$ |

Let $h(x)=f\big(g(x)\big)$, $k(x)=f(x)\,g(x)$ and $q(x)=\dfrac{f(x)}{g(x)}$.

(a) Find $h'(1)$. [2]

(b) Find $k'(2)$. [2]

(c) Find $q'(1)$. [3]

(d) Find the equation of the tangent to the graph of $h$ at the point where $x=1$. [2]

tname: Derivatives of x^n, sin, cos, e^x, ln x; chain, product and quotient rules
text:
Let $f(x)=x\sin(2x)$, for $0\le x\le\pi$.

(a) Find $f'(x)$. [2]

(b) Show that $f'\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)=1$. [2]

(c) Find the $x$-coordinates of the points on the graph of $f$, for $0<x<\pi$, where the tangent is horizontal. [3]
ms:
**(a)** $f'(x)=\sin(2x)+2x\cos(2x)$ **A1A1**

**(b)** $f'\left(\dfrac\pi4\right)=\sin\dfrac\pi2+\dfrac\pi2\cos\dfrac\pi2$ **M1**

$=1+\dfrac\pi2\times0$ **A1**

$=1$ **AG**

**(c)** $\sin(2x)+2x\cos(2x)=0$ **(M1)**

$x=1.01,\ x=2.46$ **A1A1**

Note: **FT** from their (a).

[Total 7 marks]

tname: The second derivative, concavity
text:
Let $f(x)=x^4-6x^2+2$.

(a) Find $f'(x)$ and $f''(x)$. [3]

(b) Find the values of $x$ for which the graph of $f$ is concave down. [2]

tname: The second derivative, concavity
text:
The following diagram shows the graph of $y=f'(x)$, the **derivative** of a function $f$, for $-1.2\le x\le3.5$. The graph of $f'$ touches the $x$-axis at $x=0$, crosses it at $x=3$, and has a local minimum point at $(2,\,-4)$.

![graph of y = f'(x) touching the x-axis at 0, crossing at 3, with a local minimum at (2, -4)](qbank/img/gen_math_SL5.7_2.svg)

(a) Find the $x$-coordinate of the local minimum point on the graph of $f$. Justify your answer. [2]

(b) Explain why the graph of $f$ has neither a local maximum nor a local minimum at $x=0$. [2]

(c) Write down the $x$-coordinates of the points of inflection on the graph of $f$. [2]
ms:
**(a)** $x=3$ **A1**

$f'$ changes sign from negative to positive at $x=3$ **R1**

Note: do not award **A1R0**.

**(b)** $f'(0)=0$ so the graph of $f$ has a stationary point at $x=0$ **R1**

but $f'(x)<0$ on both sides of $x=0$ (no change of sign), so it is a stationary point of inflection **R1**

**(c)** $x=0,\ x=2$ **A1A1**

Note: these are where $f'$ has turning points, so $f''$ changes sign. Award **A1A0** if extra values are given.

[Total 6 marks]

tname: The second derivative, concavity
text:
Let $f(x)=x^2\ln x$, for $x>0$.

(a) Find $f'(x)$. [2]

(b) Find $f''(x)$. [2]

(c) Find the coordinates of the point of inflection on the graph of $f$, justifying that it is a point of inflection. [3]
ms:
**(a)** $f'(x)=2x\ln x+x^2\cdot\dfrac1x=2x\ln x+x$ **A1A1**

**(b)** $f''(x)=2\ln x+2x\cdot\dfrac1x+1=2\ln x+3$ **A1A1**

**(c)** $2\ln x+3=0\Rightarrow x=\mathrm{e}^{-1.5}=0.223$ **A1**

$y=-0.0747$ (exact $-\dfrac{3}{2\mathrm{e}^3}$) **A1**

$f''(x)$ changes sign (from negative to positive) at $x=0.223$, since $\ln x$ is increasing **R1**

Note: accept justification by testing a value either side, e.g. $f''(0.1)<0$, $f''(1)>0$.

[Total 7 marks]

tname: The second derivative, concavity
text:
Let $f(x)=x^3\mathrm{e}^{-x}$, for $x\ge0$.

(a) Show that $f'(x)=x^2\mathrm{e}^{-x}(3-x)$. [2]

(b) Find the coordinates of the local maximum point on the graph of $f$. [2]

(c) Show that $f''(x)=x\mathrm{e}^{-x}\left(x^2-6x+6\right)$. [3]

(d) Find the $x$-coordinates of the points of inflection on the graph of $f$, for $x>0$. Justify your answer. [3]

(e) Find the area of the region enclosed by the graph of $f$, the $x$-axis and the line $x=3$. [2]

(f) Find the set of values of $k$ for which the equation $f(x)=k$ has exactly two solutions for $x>0$. [2]
ms:
**(a)** $f'(x)=3x^2\mathrm{e}^{-x}-x^3\mathrm{e}^{-x}$ **M1A1**

$=x^2\mathrm{e}^{-x}(3-x)$ **AG**

**(b)** $f'(x)=0\Rightarrow x=3$ (for $x>0$) **(A1)**

$(3,\ 1.34)$ (exact $(3,\ 27\mathrm{e}^{-3})$) **A1**

**(c)** $f'(x)=\mathrm{e}^{-x}\left(3x^2-x^3\right)$

$f''(x)=\mathrm{e}^{-x}\left(6x-3x^2\right)-\mathrm{e}^{-x}\left(3x^2-x^3\right)$ **M1A1**

$=\mathrm{e}^{-x}\left(x^3-6x^2+6x\right)$ **A1**

$=x\mathrm{e}^{-x}\left(x^2-6x+6\right)$ **AG**

**(d)** $x^2-6x+6=0$ **(M1)**

$x=1.27,\ x=4.73$ (exact $3\pm\sqrt3$) **A1**

$f''(x)$ changes sign at each of these values (since $x\mathrm{e}^{-x}>0$ and the quadratic factor changes sign at its distinct roots) **R1**

**(e)** $\displaystyle\int_0^3x^3\mathrm{e}^{-x}\,\mathrm{d}x$ **(M1)**

$=2.12$ **A1**

**(f)** $f(0)=0$, $f$ increases to the maximum $1.34$ at $x=3$ and then decreases towards $0$ as $x\to\infty$ **(R1)**

$0<k<1.34$ **A1**

Note: **FT** from their maximum value in (b).

[Total 14 marks]

tname: Local maxima and minima, points of inflection, optimisation
text:
A farmer builds a rectangular enclosure of area $200\ \text{m}^2$ against a long straight wall, so fencing is needed on only three sides. The two sides perpendicular to the wall each have length $x$ metres and the side parallel to the wall has length $y$ metres.

The fencing for the two perpendicular sides costs 12 dollars per metre and the fencing for the side parallel to the wall costs 8 dollars per metre. The total cost of the fencing is $C$ dollars.

(a) Show that $C=24x+\dfrac{1600}{x}$. [2]

(b) Find $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}C}{\mathrm{d}x}$. [2]

(c) Find the value of $x$ that minimizes the cost, and the minimum cost. [3]
ms:
**(a)** $xy=200\Rightarrow y=\dfrac{200}{x}$ **A1**

$C=12(2x)+8y=24x+8\times\dfrac{200}{x}$ **M1**

$=24x+\dfrac{1600}{x}$ **AG**

**(b)** $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}C}{\mathrm{d}x}=24-\dfrac{1600}{x^2}$ **A1A1**

**(c)** $24-\dfrac{1600}{x^2}=0$ (or minimum on graph of $C$) **(M1)**

$x=8.16$ m (exact $\dfrac{10\sqrt6}{3}$) **A1**

minimum cost $=392$ dollars ($391.918\ldots$) **A1**

[Total 7 marks]

tname: Local maxima and minima, points of inflection, optimisation
text:
The concentration of a drug in a patient's blood, $C\ \text{mg L}^{-1}$, $t$ hours after an injection is modelled by
$$C(t)=8t\,\mathrm{e}^{-0.4t},\quad 0\le t\le12.$$
The graph of $C$ is shown in the following diagram.

![graph of drug concentration C against time t, rising to a maximum then decreasing](qbank/img/gen_math_SL5.8_6.svg)

(a) Find $C'(t)$. [2]

(b) Find the maximum concentration and the time at which it occurs. [3]

(c) Find the time at which the concentration is decreasing most rapidly. [3]
ms:
**(a)** $C'(t)=8\mathrm{e}^{-0.4t}-3.2t\mathrm{e}^{-0.4t}$ $\left(=8\mathrm{e}^{-0.4t}(1-0.4t)\right)$ **A1A1**

**(b)** $C'(t)=0$ **(M1)**

$t=2.5$ hours **A1**

$C=7.36\ \text{mg L}^{-1}$ (exact $20\mathrm{e}^{-1}$) **A1**

**(c)** recognizing the minimum of $C'(t)$ (or $C''(t)=0$) **(M1)**

$C''(t)=\mathrm{e}^{-0.4t}(1.28t-6.4)$, so $C''(t)=0$ at $t=5$ **(A1)**

$t=5$ hours **A1**

Note: $C''(t)$ changes from negative to positive at $t=5$, and $C'(5)=-1.08$ is less than $C'(12)=-0.250$, so $t=5$ gives the most rapid decrease on $2.5<t\le12$.

[Total 8 marks]

text:
A particle moves in a straight line. Its velocity, $v\ \text{m s}^{-1}$, after $t$ seconds is given by
$$v(t)=10\mathrm{e}^{-0.5t}-3,\quad 0\le t\le6.$$
The graph of $v$ is shown in the following diagram.

![velocity-time graph decreasing from 7 and crossing the t-axis between 2 and 3](qbank/img/gen_math_SL5.9_2.svg)

(a) Write down the initial velocity of the particle. [1]

(b) Find the time at which the particle is at rest. [2]

(c) Find the acceleration of the particle when $t=1$. [2]

(d) Find the total distance travelled by the particle in the 6 seconds. [3]
ms:
**(a)** $7\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ **A1**

**(b)** $10\mathrm{e}^{-0.5t}-3=0$ **(M1)**

$t=2.41$ s (exact $2\ln\frac{10}{3}$) **A1**

**(c)** $a(t)=-5\mathrm{e}^{-0.5t}$ or using GDC **(M1)**

$a(1)=-3.03\ \text{m s}^{-2}$ **A1**

**(d)** $\displaystyle\int_0^6\left|10\mathrm{e}^{-0.5t}-3\right|\mathrm{d}t$ **(M1)(A1)**

Note: award **(M1)** for an integral of $v$, **(A1)** for the absolute value or for splitting at $t=2.41$.

$=12.5$ m **A1**

Note: $6.776\ldots+5.772\ldots=12.548\ldots$. Award **(M1)(A0)A0** for the displacement $1.00$.

[Total 8 marks]

tname: Kinematics: displacement, velocity, acceleration, distance travelled
text:
The following diagram shows the velocity–time graph for a particle moving in a straight line for $0\le t\le8$, where $v$ is in $\text{m s}^{-1}$ and $t$ is in seconds. The graph consists of three straight line segments joining $(0,\,0)$, $(2,\,6)$, $(5,\,6)$ and $(8,\,-3)$.

![piecewise linear velocity-time graph through (0,0), (2,6), (5,6) and (8,-3)](qbank/img/gen_math_SL5.9_3.svg)

(a) Find the acceleration of the particle for $0<t<2$. [1]

(b) Find the value of $t$ at which the particle changes direction. [2]

(c) Find the total distance travelled by the particle for $0\le t\le8$. [3]

(d) Find the displacement of the particle at $t=8$ from its position at $t=0$. [1]
ms:
**(a)** $\dfrac{6}{2}=3\ \text{m s}^{-2}$ **A1**

**(b)** gradient of last segment $=\dfrac{-3-6}{8-5}=-3$, so $v=6-3(t-5)$ **(M1)**

$v=0$ when $t=7$ **A1**

**(c)** area above axis $=\dfrac12(2)(6)+3(6)+\dfrac12(2)(6)=6+18+6=30$ **(M1)(A1)**

area below axis $=\dfrac12(1)(3)=1.5$

total distance $=31.5$ m **A1**

Note: accept the trapezium $\dfrac12(3+7)(6)=30$ for the area above the axis.

**(d)** $30-1.5=28.5$ m **A1**

Note: **FT** from their areas in (c).

[Total 7 marks]

tname: Kinematics: displacement, velocity, acceleration, distance travelled
text:
A particle starts from a fixed point $O$ and moves in a straight line. Its acceleration, in $\text{m s}^{-2}$, after $t$ seconds is given by $a(t)=6t-4$, for $t\ge0$. The initial velocity of the particle is $-4\ \text{m s}^{-1}$.

(a) Find an expression for the velocity, $v(t)$. [3]

(b) Find the value of $t$ when the particle is at rest. [2]

(c) Find the total distance travelled by the particle in the first 3 seconds. [4]
ms:
**(a)** $v(t)=\displaystyle\int(6t-4)\,\mathrm{d}t=3t^2-4t+c$ **(M1)A1**

$v(0)=-4\Rightarrow c=-4$, so $v(t)=3t^2-4t-4$ **A1**

**(b)** $3t^2-4t-4=0\Rightarrow(3t+2)(t-2)=0$ **(M1)**

$t=2$ (since $t\ge0$) **A1**

**(c)** $s(t)=t^3-2t^2-4t$ (as $s(0)=0$) **(M1)**

$s(2)=-8$, $s(3)=27-18-12=-3$ **(A1)(A1)**

distance $=|-8-0|+|-3-(-8)|=8+5=13$ m **A1**

Note: accept $\displaystyle-\int_0^2v\,\mathrm{d}t+\int_2^3v\,\mathrm{d}t=8+5$. Award **A0** for the displacement $-3$ or $3$.

[Total 9 marks]

tname: Kinematics: displacement, velocity, acceleration, distance travelled
text:
A particle moves in a straight line, starting from a point $O$. Its velocity, $v\ \text{m s}^{-1}$, after $t$ seconds is given by

ms:

$t=0.409,\ t=5.67$ **A1**

**(c)** $v'(t)=6\mathrm{e}^{-0.5t}-3t\mathrm{e}^{-0.5t}=0$ or maximum on graph **(M1)**

$t=2$ s **A1**

$v=2.41\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ (exact $12\mathrm{e}^{-1}-2$) **A1**

**(d)** $a(1)=v'(1)$ **(M1)**

$=1.82\ \text{m s}^{-2}$ **A1**

$=12.2$ m **A1**

$=3.03$ m **A1**

Note: **FT** from the number of sign changes of $v$ in their (b).

tname: Indefinite integration including by inspection/substitution
text:
(a) Find $\displaystyle\int x\left(x^2+1\right)^4\mathrm{d}x$. [4]

(b) Given that $f'(x)=x\left(x^2+1\right)^4$ and $f(0)=1$, find $f(x)$. [2]
ms:
**(a)** **METHOD 1** (substitution)

$u=x^2+1$, $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}u}{\mathrm{d}x}=2x$ **(M1)**

$\displaystyle\int\frac12u^4\,\mathrm{d}u$ **(A1)**

$=\dfrac{u^5}{10}+C$ **(A1)**

$=\dfrac{\left(x^2+1\right)^5}{10}+C$ **A1**

**METHOD 2** (inspection)

recognizing $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}\left(x^2+1\right)^5=10x\left(x^2+1\right)^4$ **(M1)(A1)**

$\dfrac{\left(x^2+1\right)^5}{10}+C$ **A1A1**

**(b)** $\dfrac{1^5}{10}+C=1\Rightarrow C=\dfrac9{10}$ **(M1)**

$f(x)=\dfrac{\left(x^2+1\right)^5}{10}+\dfrac{9}{10}$ **A1**

[Total 6 marks]

tname: Indefinite integration including by inspection/substitution
text:
Find

(a) $\displaystyle\int\frac{6x}{x^2+5}\,\mathrm{d}x$ [3]

(b) $\displaystyle\int\sin x\,\mathrm{e}^{\cos x}\,\mathrm{d}x$. [3]
ms:
**(a)** recognizing the numerator is a multiple of the derivative of the denominator, e.g. $u=x^2+5$, $\mathrm{d}u=2x\,\mathrm{d}x$ **(M1)**

$\displaystyle\int\frac3u\,\mathrm{d}u$ **(A1)**

$3\ln\left(x^2+5\right)+C$ **A1**

Note: accept $3\ln\left|x^2+5\right|+C$.

**(b)** $u=\cos x$, $\mathrm{d}u=-\sin x\,\mathrm{d}x$ **(M1)**

$\displaystyle-\int\mathrm{e}^u\,\mathrm{d}u$ **(A1)**

$-\mathrm{e}^{\cos x}+C$ **A1**

[Total 6 marks]

tname: Indefinite integration including by inspection/substitution
text:
(a) Find $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}\left(x\ln x\right)$, for $x>0$. [2]

(b) Hence find $\displaystyle\int\ln x\,\mathrm{d}x$. [3]

(c) Hence find the exact value of $\displaystyle\int_1^{\mathrm{e}}\ln x\,\mathrm{d}x$. [2]
ms:
**(a)** $1\times\ln x+x\times\dfrac1x$ **M1**

$=\ln x+1$ **A1**

**(b)** $\displaystyle\int(\ln x+1)\,\mathrm{d}x=x\ln x$ (+ constant) **(M1)**

$\displaystyle\int\ln x\,\mathrm{d}x=x\ln x-\int1\,\mathrm{d}x$ **(A1)**

$=x\ln x-x+C$ **A1**

**(c)** $\left[x\ln x-x\right]_1^{\mathrm{e}}=(\mathrm{e}\ln\mathrm{e}-\mathrm{e})-(1\ln1-1)$ **(M1)**

$=0-(-1)=1$ **A1**

[Total 7 marks]

tname: Definite integrals, areas between curves
text: Find the value of $\displaystyle\int_1^4\left(3\sqrt{x}-2\right)\mathrm{d}x$. [4]

tname: Definite integrals, areas between curves
text:
The following diagram shows the graphs of $y=x^2$ and $y=x+2$, which intersect at the points $P$ and $Q$. The shaded region is enclosed by the two graphs.

![parabola y = x^2 and line y = x + 2 intersecting at P and Q, region between them shaded](qbank/img/gen_math_SL5.11_2.svg)

(a) Find the $x$-coordinates of $P$ and $Q$. [3]

(b) Find the area of the shaded region. [4]
ms:
**(a)** $x^2=x+2\Rightarrow x^2-x-2=0$ **(M1)**

$(x-2)(x+1)=0$ **(A1)**

$x=-1$ (at $P$), $x=2$ (at $Q$) **A1**

**(b)** area $=\displaystyle\int_{-1}^{2}\left(x+2-x^2\right)\mathrm{d}x$ **(M1)**

$=\left[\dfrac{x^2}{2}+2x-\dfrac{x^3}{3}\right]_{-1}^{2}$ **A1**

$=\left(2+4-\dfrac83\right)-\left(\dfrac12-2+\dfrac13\right)=\dfrac{10}{3}+\dfrac76$ **(A1)**

$=\dfrac92$ **A1**

[Total 7 marks]

tname: Definite integrals, areas between curves
text:
Let $f(x)=4-x^2$ and $g(x)=\mathrm{e}^{0.5x}$. The following diagram shows the graphs of $f$ and $g$. The shaded region is enclosed by the graphs of $f$ and $g$.

**(b)** $\displaystyle\int_{-1.90}^{1.41}\left(4-x^2-\mathrm{e}^{0.5x}\right)\mathrm{d}x$ **(M1)(A1)**

tname: Definite integrals, areas between curves
text:
Let $f(x)=\dfrac{4x}{x^2+1}$, for $x\ge0$. The following diagram shows the graph of $f$ and the line $y=x$. The shaded region $R$ is enclosed by the graph of $f$ and the line $y=x$.

![graph of y = 4x/(x^2+1) and line y = x, with region R between them shaded](qbank/img/gen_math_SL5.11_5.svg)

(a) Show that $f'(x)=\dfrac{4\left(1-x^2\right)}{\left(x^2+1\right)^2}$. [3]

(b) Find the coordinates of the maximum point on the graph of $f$. Justify that it is a maximum. [3]

(c) Find the $x$-coordinates of the points where the graph of $f$ meets the line $y=x$. [3]

(d) Find the area of $R$. Give your answer in the form $a\ln2+b$, where $a,\,b\in\mathbb{Q}$. [6]
ms:
**(a)** attempt to use quotient rule **M1**

$f'(x)=\dfrac{4\left(x^2+1\right)-4x(2x)}{\left(x^2+1\right)^2}$ **A1**

$=\dfrac{4x^2+4-8x^2}{\left(x^2+1\right)^2}$ **A1**

$=\dfrac{4\left(1-x^2\right)}{\left(x^2+1\right)^2}$ **AG**

**(b)** $f'(x)=0\Rightarrow x=1$ (as $x\ge0$) **(M1)**

$(1,\ 2)$ **A1**

$f'(x)>0$ for $0\le x<1$ and $f'(x)<0$ for $x>1$, so maximum **R1**

**(c)** $\dfrac{4x}{x^2+1}=x\Rightarrow4x=x^3+x$ **M1**

$x\left(x^2-3\right)=0$ **(A1)**

$x=0,\ x=\sqrt3$ **A1**

**(d)** area $=\displaystyle\int_0^{\sqrt3}\left(\frac{4x}{x^2+1}-x\right)\mathrm{d}x$ **(M1)(A1)**

$\displaystyle\int\frac{4x}{x^2+1}\,\mathrm{d}x=2\ln\left(x^2+1\right)$ **(M1)A1**

$=\left[2\ln\left(x^2+1\right)-\dfrac{x^2}{2}\right]_0^{\sqrt3}=2\ln4-\dfrac32$ **A1**

$=4\ln2-\dfrac32$ **A1**

Note: **FT** from their limits in (c).

[Total 15 marks]

tname: Definite integrals, areas between curves
text:
Let $f(x)=3\ln(x+1)$ and $g(x)=x^2-2x$, for $0\le x\le4$. The following diagram shows the graphs of $f$ and $g$. The graphs intersect at $x=0$ and $x=b$. The shaded region $R$ is enclosed by the two graphs.

(b) Find the equation of the tangent to the graph of $f$ at the point where $x=2$. [3]

(d) Find the area of $R$. [2]

(e) Let $d(x)=f(x)-g(x)$, for $0\le x\le b$.

(i) Find $d'(x)$.

(ii) Hence find the maximum vertical distance between the graphs of $f$ and $g$ for $0\le x\le b$, and the value of $x$ at which it occurs. [6]
